title: DHS Proposes New EB-5 Rules With $1.4M Investment Tier and Tighter Oversight
excerpt: A 358-page proposed rule would codify the 2022 EB-5 Reform Act, add a new high-employment-area investment category, and impose a graduated sanctions regime on regional centers — all as a September 30 grandfathering deadline looms.
body:
• DHS published a proposed rule on July 2 to fully implement the EB-5 Reform and Integrity Act of 2022, with public comments due by August 31, 2026
  • A new $1.4 million investment minimum would apply to projects in "high employment areas," while TEA investments remain at $800,000
  • Indian investors facing years-long visa backlogs stand to benefit from a confirmed two-year capital sustainment period that limits how long their money must stay at risk

The Department of Homeland Security on July 2 published a 358-page proposed rule that would overhaul the regulations governing the EB-5 immigrant investor visa program. The notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), filed with the Federal Register by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, aims to codify the sweeping changes Congress passed in the EB-5 Reform and Integrity Act of 2022 (RIA), more than four years after President Biden signed the law.

The rule touches nearly every part of the EB-5 program — investor eligibility, regional center compliance, targeted employment area designations, priority date retention, audits, and enforcement — and introduces several provisions of DHS's own design, according to IMI Daily.

What Changes for Investors

The most notable new provision is a $1.4 million minimum investment for projects in what DHS calls "high employment areas" — parts of a metropolitan statistical area where unemployment is at least 150% below the national average. This marks the first time DHS has carved out such a category.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=yTwEZOmR4jM

Investment thresholds for targeted employment areas (TEAs), meaning rural or high-unemployment locations, remain at $800,000. The standard amount for all other locations stays at $1,050,000. All figures will be adjusted for inflation on January 1, 2027, and every five years after that.

Mona Shah, managing partner of Mona Shah & Associates Global, told IMI Daily that the new tier is unlikely to see much use. "Based on DHS's own approval data, 99.9% of regional center investors chose to invest in TEAs at the reduced amount," she said. "Very few projects will ever meet this number in the wild."

The rule also formally confirms that capital must remain at risk for a minimum of two years from the date it is made available to the job-creating entity, rather than throughout the investor's entire conditional residency. This settles a dispute that led trade association IIUSA to sue USCIS in 2024.

"The two-year sustainment period is the provision everyone has and will continue to be arguing about at conferences for the next year."

— Mona Shah, Managing Partner, Mona Shah & Associates Global

Why It Matters for Indian Investors

The two-year rule carries particular weight for Indian nationals, who alongside Chinese applicants face the longest EB-5 visa backlogs. Under the previous framework, regional centers had to "redeploy" repaid funds into new projects investors never chose, keeping money at risk for however long the backlog lasted. DHS itself expects redeployment to become rare for post-RIA petitions.

Christina Tabacco of San Francisco-based Golden Gate Global told IMI Daily she reads the provision as "a direct nod to applicants from India and China" who have historically borne the redeployment risk.

The rule also strengthens "good faith investor" protections: if a regional center is terminated or debarred, affected investors get a 180-day window to reassociate with a compliant sponsor. Their priority dates survive the move.

Tighter Oversight for Regional Centers

On the compliance side, the rule builds out a tiered penalty structure for regional centers. Violations can draw anything from a formal notice to monetary penalties of up to 10% of total capital invested, suspension, termination, and debarment. DHS floats flat fines for routine breaches — $10,000 for a late annual statement, for example.

The rule also implements mandatory audits at least every five years, fund administration requirements, and for the first time, mandatory registration of direct and third-party promoters who market EB-5 offerings abroad. DHS estimates compliance will cost each regional center roughly $47,000 per year, though Shah called that figure optimistic, noting it "leaves out costs DHS admits it could not quantify."

At least 87% of regional centers qualify as small entities, according to DHS's own analysis, and Shah warned that fixed compliance costs "always land hardest on the small, single-project centers."

What's Next

Written comments are due by August 31, 2026, after which DHS will review them and publish a final rule. The rulemaking collides with two deadlines dominating EB-5 planning: the September 30, 2026 cutoff for the RIA's grandfathering protection — which shields petitions filed before that date even if the program later lapses — and the January 1, 2027 inflation adjustment.

Petitions filed after September 30 lose that protection and could be vulnerable if Congress fails to reauthorize the regional center program beyond its current September 2027 expiration. Immigration attorneys are urging investors to file before the cutoff.

"Nobody sensible is waiting around to file," Shah predicted. "We fully expect a rush for the door, and then a rather quiet spell."
nri_angle: Indian EB-5 investors facing years-long visa backlogs stand to benefit from the confirmed two-year capital sustainment period, which limits how long their investment must remain at risk regardless of backlog length.
